In infants with mild toxoplasmosis, some experts recommend alter- nating pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine with spiramycin on a monthly basis from months 7 to 12, in order to reduce the risk of bone marrow suppression. However, infants with HIV infection and moderate to severe toxoplasmosis should receive the full 12-month regimen of pyrimeth- amine-sulfadiazine.7 Longer courses of treatment may be given in cases of extensive disease. A corticosteroid, usu- ally dexamethasone or prednisolone, has been added in children with CNS involvement.7 In immunocompetent individuals, ocular toxoplasmosis is a self-limiting disease and requires no treatment, unless visual acuity is threatened or there is a large retinal lesion with marked vitritis.10-12 A systematic review13 found a lack of evidence to support routine treatment for acute tox- oplasma retinochoroiditis in immunocompetent patients, but did find weak evidence to suggest that long-term treat- ment of patients with chronic recurrent disease may reduce recurrence. All immunocompromised patients should be treated and prolonged treatment is necessary to prevent re- crudescence. The best drug regimen is unknown. The most commonly used regimens are pyrimethamine with sulfadi- azine or pyrimethamine with clindamycin (which is con- centrated in the choroid). Benefit has been reported from clindamycin with corticosteroids,14 although corticoster- oids should never be used alone since fulminant cases may occur. Spiramycin is not indicated for ocular toxoplasmo- sis. Prophylaxis. Primary prophylaxis against T. gondii infec- tion has been investigated in AIDS patients and recipients of organ transplants. In HIV-infected persons who are se- ropositive for Toxoplasma and who have a CD4+ T lym- phocyte count of less than 100 cells/microlitre, primary prophylaxis against encephalitis should be given.15 Co-tri- moxazole, in regimens designed for pneumocystis pneu- monia prophylaxis, was found to be effective and is there- fore recommended.15 Alternatively, pyrimethamine plus dapsone may be given.15 Atovaquone with or without py- rimethamine can also be considered.15 Pyrimethamine plus sulfadoxine has also been tried, with promising re- sults.16 Toxoplasma-seronegative persons who are not re- ceiving a pneumocystis prophylactic regimen known to be active against toxoplasmic encephalitis should be retested for Toxoplasma should their CD4+ T lymphocyte count fall below 100 cells/microlitre and if they have serocon- verted primary prophylaxis should be instigated.15 Prima-
